$comment: AGENTS.md 2.3: every @Public use is listed here with its justification, so exemptions are reviewable rather than invisible. check-route-guards.mjs fails when the decorator and this file disagree in EITHER direction - a route with no entry, or an entry whose route no longer exists. An unreconciled allowlist decays into a historical document and stops constraining anything.

routes.reason: The signed certificate IS the credential, exactly as the setup token is on POST /auth/setup/complete: a deployment being licensed for the first time has no session to authorise with, and the first administrator (created by setup) holds no roles, so any permission gate would be unreachable. The authorisation is the ECDSA P-256 signature over the canonical payload (ADR-009), producible only by the holder of the licence private key, plus a binding to THIS school - a certificate naming another school is refused before anything is stored. The route grants nothing itself: it validates, binds, persists and refreshes the cache, and only a stored certificate changes what EntitlementGuard refuses. Three refusals (forged, wrong school, expired) answer one frozen 400 so a probing caller learns nothing, and the audit record plus the log carry the detail. Bounded by verification cost, by one licence row per school, and by @Audited('LICENCE_ACTIVATION'). AGENTS.md 2.3, 2.13.

A caller who has forgotten a password has no session to be authorised against - that is the entire population this route serves. The action is bounded instead: the account is resolved by email with one indexed read that answers identically for a missing identifier (so the route is not an enumeration oracle), a valid ACTIVE account is required before any credential is minted, the response body is a CONSTANT 200 whether or not an account exists, and a per-source throttle bounds outbound mail so one caller cannot spend the school's SMTP quota and get the domain blacklisted. A suspended account receives nothing at all - a reset link would be a way around the suspension. No @RequireEntitlement, because recovering a credential is not a licensed feature: an edition that cannot reset a password is an edition that cannot be used. @Audited('PASSWORD_RESET_REQUEST') writes its row (PLT-402) with no email and no body content. AGENTS.md 2.3, 2.13, 2.14.

The reset token IS the credential on this route, exactly as it is on POST /auth/setup/complete: it is single-use (the redemption is one guarded UPDATE whose row count is the decision, not a read-then-write), time-limited from PASSWORD_RESET_TTL_MS, and stored only as a SHA-256 hash, so a reader of the table cannot replay it. It consumes nothing until the password policy accepts the candidate, so a weak password cannot burn a link. There is no session to gate with - the caller is someone who cannot sign in - so a permission check would gate the very recovery the route exists to provide. It is bounded by the token, by argon2id at the school's configured cost, and by the password policy, and every refusal (forged, used, expired) answers one byte-identical frozen 400 so a caller probing links learns nothing. A successful reset consumes the token, writes the new hash, and revokes every prior session (AC-2, revokeAllForUser). @Audited('PASSWORD_RESET_CONFIRM') writes its row (PLT-402). AGENTS.md 2.3, 2.13.

Starts a Google OIDC sign-in. It is the only route a browser can reach before a session exists, so a permission check here would require the permission the route exists to obtain. It grants nothing and changes nothing: no session, no row, no school data, no role consulted. Hence no @RequireEntitlement, and no @Audited - the audit record belongs on GET /auth/oidc/callback, where a stranger's assertion becomes a local account. AGENTS.md 2.3 and 2.13.

The one-time setup token IS the credential on this route. A permission check would require the permission the route exists to grant: no account, session or role exists before the token is spent, and the deployment state it reads is precisely what a permission system cannot gate. It is the only UNAUTHENTICATED WRITE in the system, and it is bounded by three things that are all independent of RBAC: the token itself (256 bits of CSPRNG, stored only as SHA-256, single-use, inside one transaction with the credential write), argon2id (so a guess costs tens of milliseconds and 19 MiB), and a per-source throttle that answers 429. @Audited('SETUP_COMPLETE') now writes its row (PLT-402, the AuditInterceptor, since 2026-10-11). AGENTS.md 2.3, 2.13, 2.14.

Sign-in is how a session is obtained, so a permission check would require the permission the route exists to grant - the same circularity as the OIDC redirect, and the reason D57 makes this route MANDATORY rather than a fallback: Google must-link, so a session is the only way anything can be linked. Unlike the redirect this route does change state, because it issues a session; what makes the exemption safe is scope rather than inertness - it acts only on the caller, only on a credential they presented, and only when that credential verifies. No other account is read or written, no role is consulted, no school data is reachable. No @RequireEntitlement, because a Basic-edition school must still be able to sign in or it cannot use the product at all. @Audited('LOGIN') now writes one row per outcome (PLT-402): success and failure both, and the constraint recorded in the controller is that a failure record must carry no identifier and no credential, or the audit log becomes the enumeration oracle the route exists to prevent. AGENTS.md 2.3, 2.13.

Sign-in is how a session is obtained, so a permission check would require the permission the route exists to grant: no account, session or role exists before a verified identity is resolved, and D57 makes the ExternalIdentity lookup the authorisation. What makes this exemption safe where it would be fatal on almost any other route is that the route CANNOT LINK. The naive design - 'if a session cookie is present, link, otherwise sign in' - is account takeover: a victim is signed in, an attacker starts a Google sign-in in the victim's browser and completes it with their OWN Google account, and the callback binds the attacker's identity to the victim's account. So the flow mode is decided by the route that BEGAN the flow, sealed inside the HMAC-signed OIDC state cookie, and this handler takes no session cookie, no userId and no code path that could produce one. Only GET /auth/oidc/link, which sits behind the globally-registered SessionGuard, can seal link mode - and it names the account inside the MAC too, so the callback never has to trust the session to decide what to link. Every one of the nine refusals (absent bundle, forged bundle, expired bundle, state mismatch, provider rejection, all four D49 domain refusals, unverified email, unlinked identity, identity bound elsewhere) answers 401 with one byte-identical body, so the route is not an oracle about which states are real or which identities exist; the typed reason is retained for the log and the audit record. A forged or expired state is refused BEFORE any network call. D57 additionally forbids auto-provisioning, so an unknown subject is refused and NOTHING is created - auto-creating a User for any verified @school.lk address would let any student with a school Gmail become a system user. No @RequireEntitlement, because a Basic-edition school must still be able to sign in. @Audited('OIDC_CALLBACK') now writes its row (PLT-402). AGENTS.md 2.3, 2.13; D57, D48, D49, D60.
